$comment: The analytics contract, shared by both platforms — the same role
weather-slot-matrix.json plays for the weather mapper. Signal names and
payload keys are implemented twice (TypeScript and Swift), so without a
fixture the two dashboards would silently diverge into two vocabularies
and the numbers would stop being comparable. Both suites assert their own
Unlike the slot matrix this one is hand-authored, not generated: it is a
contract being chosen, not a computation being captured. Edit it
deliberately, and expect both suites to go red until both platforms agree.
payloadKeyAllowlist is the privacy boundary, and it is enforced by test on
both platforms. City names, search queries, coordinates and world names are
all absent by design. Slot IDs answer the same product question using
generic weather vocabulary, and carry none of the catalog's IP exposure.

signals.name: App.launched
signals.answers: Did someone come back. Combined with the durable client ID, this alone yields retention.

signals.answers: Did the core path work at all, and which weather people actually get.

signals.name: Atlas.worldAssigned
signals.answers: Intent. The gap between opened and assigned is the interesting number.

signals.name: Passport.stampEarned
signals.answers: Did the collection loop actually engage anyone.

signals.name: Premium.paywallShown
signals.answers: The denominator for purchases. App Store Connect reports sales but cannot report who saw the offer and declined. `context` is which gate sent them there — a locked world, a second world on one slot, or saved locations — so a low conversion rate can be attributed to a gate rather than to the price.
